María sonrió, negando con la cabeza. 


— Todavía no me acostumbro al título, Hugo. Suena 
demasiado serio. 


Hugo les entregó unas carpetas negras con un logotipo 
plateado en relieve. 


— La Fundación ha completado la compra del antiguo 
astillero militar en Vigo. Ya es nuestro. Será vuestra base 
operativa permanente. Tecnología punta, acceso directo 
al Atlántico y jurisdicción internacional para operaciones 


de patrimonio subacuático. 
Lucas saltó de alegría, casi tirando las carpetas. 


— ¡Vamos a tener un submarino! ¡Hugo me ha prometido 
un submarino amarillo! ¡Como los Beatles! ¡Vamos a vivir 
en un submarino amarillo! 


— No será amarillo, Lucas, por el amor de Dios 
—corrigió Hugo con una sonrisa paciente—. Será negro 
táctico. Y tendrá una IA mejor que la de Iron Man. 


María abrió la carpeta. En la primera página, el logotipo 
de la nueva agencia: UPS (Unidad de Patrimonio 
Subacuático). Y debajo, su nombre: María Souto. 
Directora de Operaciones. 


— Hay mucho trabajo ahí fuera —dijo Hugo, mirando al 
horizonte donde el cielo se juntaba con el agua—. 
Barcos de esclavos hundidos que necesitan ser 
recordados, galeones españoles llenos de historia, 
ciudades perdidas bajo el hielo... El mar está lleno de 
secretos, María. Y alguien tiene que protegerlos de los 
nuevos Victor Barrows que vendrán. 


María cerró la carpeta. Respiró hondo el aire de Galicia, 
ese aire que olía a sal, a algas, a lluvia y a hogar. Sintió 
el peso de los años caer de sus hombros. 


Miró a Erik, el hermano que eligió. A Lucas, el genio 


inocente. A Hugo, el redentor. Su familia. 


Miró al mar, ese inmenso monstruo azul que le había 
quitado tanto —a su padre, a Iñigo— y que ahora, por 
fin, le devolvía un propósito. 


— ¿Estamos listos? —preguntó María. 


Erik se limpió las manos en el pantalón y sonrió, con esa 
lealtad inquebrantable en la mirada. 


— Siempre. ¿A dónde vamos? 


María se ajustó la chaqueta, sintiéndose completa por 
primera vez en mucho tiempo. Echó a andar hacia el 
coche, seguida por su equipo. 


— Pues vamos. La marea está subiendo. Y hay un 
mundo entero esperando ahí abajo.

SINOPSIS 


Victor Barrows ha regresado de entre los muertos con una 
sed de venganza capaz de incendiar Europa. Aliado con la 
organización criminal Nexus, busca el tesoro más codiciado 
de la antigiiedad: la Nave Perdida de Tarsis. Ya no se trata 
solo de oro, sino de una carrera contra el tiempo por 
controlar una tecnología olvidada y letal que podria 
desestabilizar el orden mundial. 


Con su base reducida a cenizas y perseguidos por la justicia 
internacional, la inspectora María Souto y su equipo deben 
dejar de huir para convertirse en cazadores. Desde las minas 
sangrientas de Riotinto hasta el lujo corrupto de Mykonos y 
las selvas de la Triple Frontera, librarán una guerra global en 
las sombras para limpiar su nombre y detener la inminente 
catástrofe. 


El desenlace aguarda a seiscientos metros bajo el mar 
Tirreno, en la boca de un volcán dormido. En un descenso 
suicida hacia el abismo, María descubrirá que el verdadero 
legado de Tarsis no es la riqueza, sino un secreto capaz de 
reescribir la historia, y que el mar, en su eterna justicia, 
siempre exige un sacrificio para devolver lo que es suyo.

Beyond mentoring: social 
support structures for young 
Austraiian carpentry apprentices 

John Buchanan, Catherine Raffaele, Nick Giozier 
and Aran Kanagaratnam 


a 


www.ncver.edu.au/ 

pubiications/2865.htmi 


This study is an exploration of the work-based social support structures associated with 
the transition from school to work for young people and how these could, potentially, 
contribute to better mental health and wellbeing outcomes. Research and policy 
concerning young adults and mental health tends to focus on ‘at risk’ individuals; this 
project, however, examines more broadly the important role of the workplace as a 
potential site of social support. It also draws on and contributes to broader debates 
about the apprenticeship model in Australia and notions of vocational development. The 
findings have been generated from a literature review and eight case studies involving 
both small and large organisations across some of Australia’s leading firms and group 
training organisations, specifically those with apprentice completion rates sitting at 
around 90%, well above the industry average. The report identifies the forms of social 
support successfully provided to young carpentry apprentices. 

Key messages 

• Informal and peer-based mentoring practices play a significant role in supporting the 
mental health and wellbeing of apprentices and are often superior to those provided 
under a formal mentoring arrangement. The paradox is that these practices are hard 
to ‘formally’ nurture; however, employers can create environments in which they 
can succeed. 

• The essential ingredient is a quality approach to vocational development, which 
both large and small organisations can foster by: 

- valuing the time required for both on- and off-the-job training 

- ensuring supervisors and peers recognise that skills development takes time and 
requires active nurturing on the job 

- placing high value on sharing skills and teamwork 

- respecting and placing importance on time for innovation 

- encouraging apprentices to tap into wider support networks 

- ensuring access to both formal and informal mentoring. 

• Creating informal support structures works best when the arrangements are integral, 
not incidental, to the busi

CHRONOLOGICAL CLASSIFICATION 
OF THE MYCONIAN COINS BY STYLE 


As the reader sees, we classified the Myconian coins in nine classes 
(A’- ©’), using as a guide this very style of the coins. Indeed, those of 
the class A’, the most ancient of all, are characterized by the almost ar- 
chaic form of Dionysus with pointed beard.' Immediately after these 
we have the class B’ where the god is depicted with rolled hair of ar- 
chaic style. Then follow the coins of I”, with similar but ruder types 
and Dionysus with a thicker beard. The class A’ presents the same 
types again but much more artful, the hair of the god being unbound 
and without braids. With the class E’ the art approaches its highest 
peak, while the type of Dionysus’ head is transformed to a beardless 
one and, on the bigger coins, is not turned to the right but facing; the 
coins are comparable to the best of Amphipolis and Rhodes. In the 
next class C’ the obverse type declines to an artless copy of the previ- 
ous class, and next to the grape and the corn grain, permanently 
found on all previous classes, a thyrsus is added. In the class Z’ 
Dionysus’ head remains unchanged, but almost barbarized, but with 
the class H’ a totally new period begins. The permanent type of the 
grape, on the coins of all previous classes, is replaced by a double ear 
of corn and the inscription

COINS STRUCK IN MYCONOS, DELOS AND TENOS 
BEFORE THE GRECO-PERSIAN WARS 


During the years of the great acme of the Cyclades and mostly 
from the first years of the invention of the coinage at the dawn of the 
7th century B.C. many silver coins were struck; at the islands of the 
Ionian settlers the Aeginetic standard was used, while the Dorians 
used the Phoenician standard. Aglaosthenes of Naxos testifies in his 
book Naxiaca that it was the Naxians who first struck coins and not the 
Aeginetans or the Lydians, as it is generally believed.'’ Of course the 
surviving Naxian coins do not seem to be so ancient as the first Aegi- 
netic or Lydian ones, but there is a didrachm attributed to Naxos on 
which is depicted the most ancient type of human figure ona coin; this 
piece was found in Thera and bears the head of a Silenus.’* Such a 
coin perhaps had in mind Aglaosthenes and, ignoring that the types 
of animals are older, was led to the above conjecture. 

Until now many archaic Cycladic coins have been found, notably 
on these very islands. So, in 1821 a hoard of 760 silver coins was found 
in Thera island, the most of them didrachms, registered in detail by 
H.P. Borell,'° and later discussed by Wroth in his article “The Santorin 
find of 1821”.4 A similar find emerged a few years later in Melos, and 
a third one equally important was recently described by Greenwell 
in his paper “On a find of archaic Greek coins of the islands of the 
Aegean sea”.'° Unfortunately these coins are anepigraphic, so their 
classification is very difficult and only a part of them were recognized 
as belonging to various Cycladic islands; the rest were characterized

MYTHOLOGY AND COIN TYPES 


As it is easily seen in the Plates and the Catalogue, the main type is 
the grape — mostly denoting the jocular element of the island; and, in- 
deed, the wines of the island are still its main product and a famous 
one in the antiquity.” Plinius includes the Myconian wine in the very 
best.” As a natural consequence, Dionysus was the prominently wor- 
shipped god. His ivy-wreathed head or bust were the main types of 
the obverse of all coins struck after the Greco-Persian Wars, on which 
the grape of the pre-war struck coins is transferred to the reverse as 
the main type followed by the Dionysiac thyrsus. On the coins of the 
years of Augustus, Dionysus is standing, naked, holding a phiale and 
a thyrsus, probably copying his main statue in the island. In the im- 
portant decree of sacrifices we read that Semele, his mother, and him- 
self as Baccheus and Lenaeus were also worshipped and because of it 
two of the months were locally called Bacchion and Lenaeon. Even 
more the mythological traditions of the island relate its archegetes 
Myconus to Dionysus, because Myconus was the son of Anius who 
was the father of Thasos and Andros, i.e. the archegetes of the homo- 
nymous islands, where Dionysus was par excellence worshipped, but 
he also was the father of the famous Oenotropoi of Delos, i.e. Spermo, 
Oeno and Elais, to whom their grandfather Dionysus “éyapioato 
onote Bobdoivto oivov, onéppata Kai Edaiov noleiv Kai LapBavelv” 
[= gave the gift of producing and getting wine, corn and olive oil whenever 
they want]. Anius’ parents were Apollo and the nymph Rhoeo. 


(*) Not any more, of course! Unfortunately, today the biggest part of the island is 
covered of hotels and other touristic settlements; no place, time and vein for viticul- 
ture. As far as it concerns the agricultural production, the reader should keep in mind 
that the original text was wrtitten at the end of the 19th century.
